title: Masala Dosa
desc: A crisp, golden rice-and-lentil crepe wrapped around a turmeric-spiced potato filling.
ingredients: 2 cups dosa batter (fermented rice & urad dal, store-bought or homemade)
1 tbsp oil, plus extra for the tawa
steps: Make the potato filling first: heat 1 tbsp oil in a pan and add the mustard seeds. Let them pop for a few seconds, then add the curry leaves and green chillies and fry for 10 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced onion and cook over medium heat for 4-5 minutes, stirring now and then, until it turns soft and translucent.

Sprinkle in the turmeric powder and salt, then add the boiled potato cubes. Mash the potatoes lightly with the back of your spoon so some pieces break down and thicken the mix while others stay chunky. Cook for 3-4 minutes so the flavours combine, then set the filling aside and keep it warm.

Heat a flat tawa or non-stick pan on medium-high heat. Once hot, reduce to medium and lightly grease the surface with a few drops of oil, wiping it with a folded cloth or tissue so only a thin film remains.
Pour a ladle of dosa batter in the centre and spread it outward in a circular motion using the back of the ladle, working from the centre outwards to get a thin, even, roughly 10-inch circle.
Drizzle 1/2 tsp oil around the edges and on top. Cook undisturbed for 2-3 minutes until the underside turns golden brown and crisp and the top looks dry — dosas are only cooked on one side.
Spoon a portion of the potato filling onto one half of the dosa, then fold the other half over it, or fold in both sides for the classic rolled shape. Slide it off the tawa onto a plate.
Repeat with the remaining batter and filling. Serve immediately while crisp, with coconut chutney and sambar on the side.

title: Vegetable Poha
desc: Flattened rice tossed with peanuts, curry leaves, and vegetables — light, fast, everyday breakfast.
steps: Place the poha in a colander and rinse briefly under running water — just enough to soften it, about 20-30 seconds. Do not soak it or it will turn mushy. Set aside to drain and soften for 5 minutes; it should be tender but still holding its shape.
Heat oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the peanuts and fry for 2 minutes until they turn a shade darker and smell toasted, then push them to the side of the pan.
Add the mustard seeds to the same oil and let them pop, then add the curry leaves and green chillies and fry for 10 seconds.
Add the diced potato, cover the pan, and cook for 6-7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potato is fork-tender.
Add the chopped onion and cook for 2-3 minutes until it softens slightly. Sprinkle in the turmeric powder and salt, stirring to coat everything evenly.

Add the softened poha to the pan in stages, using a light folding motion with a wide spatula rather than stirring hard, so the delicate flakes don't break apart. Cook for 2-3 minutes just to heat the poha through and let it absorb the spices.
Turn off the heat, squeeze over the lemon juice, and scatter the chopped coriander on top. Fold gently once more and serve warm.

title: Rajma Chawal
desc: Red kidney beans simmered in a thick tomato-onion gravy, served over steamed rice — a North Indian lunch staple.
ingredients: 1.5 cups rajma (red kidney beans), soaked overnight
2 cups cooked steamed rice, to serve
steps: Drain the soaked rajma and pressure-cook it with 3 cups of fresh water and a pinch of salt for about 6-8 whistles, or until the beans are completely soft and can be mashed easily between two fingers. Set aside, keeping the cooking liquid.
Heat oil or ghee in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for a few seconds until fragrant.
Add the chopped onions and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until they turn a deep golden brown — this base flavour is what gives the curry its depth, so don't rush this step.
Stir in the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute until the raw smell disappears.

Add the pureed tomatoes along with the coriander powder, red chilli powder, and salt. Cook this masala for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the oil begins to separate at the edges of the pan — a sign the raw tomato taste has cooked out.
Add the cooked rajma along with its cooking liquid. Mash a few of the beans against the side of the pot with your spoon to naturally thicken the gravy.
Cover partially and simmer on low heat for 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the gravy thickens to a rich, clinging consistency and the beans are infused with the masala.
Sprinkle in the garam masala, stir, and simmer for 2 more minutes. Garnish with chopped coriander and serve hot spooned over steamed rice.

title: Paneer Butter Masala
desc: Soft paneer cubes in a velvety, mildly sweet tomato-cashew gravy finished with butter and cream.
ingredients: 1 tsp kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves), crushed
steps: Place the chopped tomatoes, onion, and cashews in a small pan with half a cup of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 10 minutes until the tomatoes turn completely soft and the onion is translucent.
Let this mixture cool slightly, then blend it to a completely smooth paste in a blender. Pass it through a sieve if you'd like an extra silky, restaurant-style gravy.
Heat 1 tbsp of the butter in a pan over medium heat. Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute until fragrant.

Pour in the blended tomato-cashew paste carefully, as it may splutter. Add the Kashmiri chilli powder and salt, and cook the gravy for 10-12 minutes on medium-low heat, stirring often, until it thickens and the raw tomato smell is completely gone.
Add the sugar to balance the acidity of the tomatoes, and stir in the crushed kasuri methi.
Gently slide in the paneer cubes and simmer for 4-5 minutes so they soak up the gravy — avoid stirring too vigorously so the cubes stay intact.
Stir in the fresh cream and the remaining tablespoon of butter, then sprinkle over the garam masala. Simmer for another 2 minutes on low heat.
Turn off the heat and serve hot with naan, roti, or steamed rice.

title: Dal Tadka
desc: Yellow lentils simmered soft and finished with a sizzling ghee tempering of garlic, cumin, and dried chilli.
steps: Rinse both dals together until the water runs clear, then add them to a pressure cooker with the chopped tomato, turmeric, salt, and 3 cups of water.

Pressure-cook for 4-5 whistles, or until the lentils are completely soft and have broken down into a thick, porridge-like consistency. If cooking on the stovetop instead, simmer covered for 30-35 minutes, topping up water as needed.

Once cooked, whisk the dal briskly with a whisk or the back of a ladle to smooth it out to your preferred consistency — some like it slightly textured, others silky smooth. Add a splash of hot water if it's too thick, and keep it warm on low heat.
For the tempering, heat the ghee in a small pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for a few seconds.
Add the sliced garlic and dried red chillies, and fry for 1-2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the garlic turns golden brown and crisp — watch closely as it can burn quickly.
Turn off the heat, add the red chilli powder and asafoetida, and stir for a couple of seconds — the residual heat is enough to cook the spices without burning them.
Immediately pour this hot, sizzling tempering over the warm dal. Cover the pot for a minute to let the aroma infuse, then stir it through.
Garnish with chopped coriander and serve hot with steamed rice or roti.

title: Baingan Bharta
desc: Fire-roasted eggplant mashed and cooked down with onions, tomatoes, and spices — smoky and comforting.
ingredients: 3 tbsp mustard oil or regular oil
steps: Rub a little oil all over the whole eggplant and pierce it in a few places with a fork so it doesn't burst while cooking. Roast it directly over an open flame on the stovetop, turning every couple of minutes with tongs, until the skin is completely charred and blackened all over and the flesh feels soft — about 12-15 minutes. If you don't have a gas flame, roast it in an oven at 220°C for 30-35 minutes, turning halfway.

Let the roasted eggplant cool enough to handle, then peel off the charred skin under running water or by hand — a bit of char left behind is fine, as it adds a smoky flavour. Mash the soft flesh roughly with a fork and set it aside.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. If using mustard oil, heat it until it just starts to smoke lightly, then reduce the heat — this cooks off its raw sharpness.
Add the chopped onions and green chillies, and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onions turn golden brown.
Stir in the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute until fragrant, then add the chopped tomatoes, turmeric, red chilli powder, and salt.
Cook the tomato mixture for 8-10 minutes, mashing the tomatoes with your spatula as they soften, until the oil starts to separate at the edges of the pan.

Add the mashed eggplant to the pan and mix well, letting it cook together with the masala for 8-10 minutes on medium-low heat, stirring frequently, until everything comes together into a thick, jammy mixture.
Sprinkle in the garam masala, stir, and cook for another 2 minutes. Finish with chopped coriander and serve hot with roti.

title: Idli Sambar
desc: Steamed rice-lentil cakes, soft as a cloud, served with a tangy lentil-vegetable sambar.
ingredients: 2 cups idli batter (fermented rice & urad dal)
steps: Grease the idli moulds lightly with oil, pour the batter into each cavity until three-quarters full, and steam in an idli steamer or a covered pot with a rack for 10-12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.
Meanwhile, pressure-cook the toor dal with turmeric and 2 cups water for 3-4 whistles until soft, then whisk it smooth.
In a separate pot, boil the drumstick, carrot, pumpkin, and onion with the tamarind paste and sambar powder in 2 cups water until the vegetables are tender, about 10 minutes.
Stir the cooked dal into the vegetable mixture, add salt, and simmer for 8-10 minutes until it thickens into a stew-like consistency.
For the tempering, heat oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, add the curry leaves and asafoetida, and pour the sizzling tempering over the sambar.
Unmould the idlis once firm and serve hot with the sambar and coconut chutney on the side.

title: Aloo Paratha
desc: Whole wheat flatbread stuffed with spiced mashed potato, cooked until golden with ghee.
steps: Knead the flour with water and a pinch of salt into a soft dough, cover, and let it rest for 20 minutes.
Mix the mashed potato with onion, green chilli, cumin powder, red chilli powder, amchur, coriander, and salt until well combined.
Divide the dough and potato filling into equal balls. Roll a dough ball into a small disc, place the filling in the centre, gather the edges up and seal.
Dust with flour and gently roll the stuffed ball out into a paratha about 7 inches wide, taking care not to let the filling burst through.
Cook on a hot tawa for a minute until bubbles appear, flip, and spread ghee on both sides, pressing gently with a spatula until golden brown patches appear on each side.
Repeat with the remaining dough and filling. Serve hot with yogurt, butter, and pickle.

title: Chole Masala
desc: Chickpeas simmered in a bold, tangy onion-tomato masala — the heart of a good chole bhature.
ingredients: Chopped coriander and sliced onion, to garnish
steps: Pressure-cook the soaked chickpeas with the tea bag and a pinch of salt in 3 cups water for 6-8 whistles until soft, then discard the tea bag and set the chickpeas aside with their liquid.
Heat oil in a pot, add the chopped onions, and cook for 8-10 minutes until deep golden brown.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add the pureed tomatoes, chole masala powder, red chilli powder, and salt.
Cook the masala for 10 minutes, stirring often, until the oil separates at the edges of the pan.
Add the cooked chickpeas along with their liquid, mash a few against the pot to thicken the gravy, and simmer for 15-20 minutes until thick and richly flavoured.
Garnish with coriander and sliced onion, and serve hot with bhature or steamed rice.

title: Vegetable Biryani
desc: Fragrant basmati rice layered with spiced mixed vegetables and slow-cooked to let the flavours mingle.
ingredients: 2 cups mixed vegetables (carrot, beans, peas, cauliflower)
1 onion, thinly sliced and fried crisp
A few saffron strands soaked in warm milk
3 tbsp ghee, Whole spices (bay leaf, cardamom, cinnamon)
steps: Cook the soaked rice in plenty of salted boiling water with the whole spices until it's about 70% cooked, then drain and set aside.
Heat ghee in a heavy pot, add the ginger-garlic paste, and cook briefly before adding the mixed vegetables. Sauté for 5-6 minutes.
Stir in the yogurt, biryani masala, and salt, and cook the vegetables for 8-10 minutes until just tender and coated in a thick masala.
Layer half the parboiled rice over the vegetable masala, scatter over half the fried onions, mint, and coriander, then repeat with the remaining rice and toppings.
Drizzle the saffron milk over the top, cover the pot tightly with a lid (sealing the edge with dough if needed), and cook on very low heat for 20-25 minutes to let the flavours steam through.
Let the biryani rest for 5 minutes off the heat before gently fluffing and serving with raita.

title: Palak Paneer
desc: Soft paneer cubes bathed in a smooth, vibrant spinach gravy, lightly spiced and finished with cream.
steps: Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 2 minutes, then plunge it into ice water to keep its colour. Blend it with the green chillies to a smooth puree.
Heat oil in a pan, add the onion, and cook for 5-6 minutes until soft, then add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook for 6-8 minutes until they break down completely and the oil separates.
Stir in the spinach puree and salt, and simmer for 6-8 minutes on low heat, stirring occasionally so it doesn't stick.
Gently add the paneer cubes and garam masala, and simmer for 4-5 minutes so the paneer absorbs the flavours.
Swirl in the cream, simmer for another minute, and serve hot with roti or rice.

title: Malai Kofta
desc: Deep-fried potato-paneer dumplings served in a rich, creamy cashew-tomato gravy.
ingredients: 2 tomatoes, 8 cashews, 1 onion — for the gravy
steps: Mix the mashed potato, grated paneer, cornflour, and salt into a smooth dough. Shape into small balls, pressing a few chopped cashews into the centre of each.
Heat oil for deep-frying to medium-hot and fry the koftas in batches, turning gently, until golden brown all over. Drain on paper towels.
For the gravy, boil the tomatoes, onion, and cashews in water for 10 minutes until soft, then blend to a smooth paste.
Heat a little oil, add the ginger-garlic paste, cook briefly, then pour in the blended paste along with garam masala and salt. Simmer for 10-12 minutes until thick.
Stir in the cream and simmer for 2 more minutes on low heat.
Just before serving, place the koftas in a serving dish and pour the hot gravy over them — adding them too early will make them soggy.

title: Samosa
desc: Crisp, flaky pastry triangles stuffed with spiced potato and peas — the classic Indian teatime snack.
ingredients: 4 tbsp ghee, plus more for frying
steps: Rub the ghee into the flour with a pinch of salt until it resembles breadcrumbs, then knead in cold water gradually to form a stiff dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Heat a little ghee in a pan, add cumin seeds, then the peas and green chilli, and cook for 3-4 minutes.
Add the potato cubes, garam masala, amchur, and salt, mashing lightly as you mix so the filling holds together while staying chunky. Let it cool.
Divide the dough into balls, roll each into an oval, and cut in half. Fold each half into a cone, sealing the straight edge with water.
Fill each cone with the potato mixture, then seal the top edge firmly to form a triangle.
Heat oil for deep-frying to medium-low and fry the samosas slowly for 12-15 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden and crisp all over. Serve hot with tamarind or mint chutney.

title: Pav Bhaji
desc: A buttery mash of mixed vegetables in a spiced tomato base, served with toasted, buttered pav buns.
ingredients: 3 potatoes, 1 cup cauliflower, 1/2 cup peas, 1 capsicum — chopped
1 onion, finely chopped, plus extra for garnish
Lemon wedges and coriander, to serve
steps: Boil the potatoes, cauliflower, and peas together until completely soft, then mash roughly and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp butter in a wide pan, add the chopped onion, and cook for 5 minutes until soft, then add the capsicum and cook for 3 more minutes.
Add the chopped tomatoes, pav bhaji masala, red chilli powder, and salt, and cook for 10 minutes, mashing the tomatoes down, until the mixture turns jammy.
Add the mashed vegetables along with a splash of water, and simmer for 10-12 minutes, mashing continuously with a potato masher, until the bhaji is thick and smooth.
Split the pav buns and toast them on a griddle with a smear of butter until golden on both sides.
Top the bhaji with a knob of butter and serve hot with the buttered pav, chopped onion, and lemon wedges.

title: Dhokla
desc: Steamed, spongy gram flour cakes from Gujarat, tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves.
ingredients: 1 tsp fruit salt (ENO) or baking soda
steps: Whisk the besan, semolina, yogurt, ginger-green chilli paste, sugar, salt, and enough water into a smooth, thick-but-pourable batter.
Grease a steaming tin. Just before steaming, stir the fruit salt into the batter along with a teaspoon of water — it will fizz and become airy, so pour it into the tin right away.
Steam the batter in a covered steamer for 15-18 minutes until a toothpick inserted comes out clean and the top springs back when pressed.
Let it cool slightly, then cut into squares while still in the tin.
For the tempering, heat oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, add the curry leaves, and pour over 1/4 cup water to make a light syrup.
Pour the tempering evenly over the dhokla squares and let them soak it up for a few minutes before serving with green chutney.

title: Gulab Jamun
desc: Soft milk-solid dumplings, deep-fried golden and soaked in warm rose-cardamom sugar syrup.
ingredients: 1 cup khoya (milk solids) or milk powder
steps: Boil the sugar and water together with the crushed cardamom for 8-10 minutes until you have a one-string consistency syrup, then stir in the rose water and keep the syrup warm.
Knead the khoya, flour, and baking soda together, adding a little milk at a time, into a soft, smooth, crack-free dough.
Divide the dough into small balls, rolling each between your palms until completely smooth — any cracks will cause the jamuns to split while frying.

Heat oil or ghee on low-medium heat (it should be barely warm when the balls go in) and fry the jamuns slowly, moving them gently, until they turn a deep, even brown all over — about 8-10 minutes; frying too hot will leave them raw inside.
Drain the fried jamuns and drop them straight into the warm sugar syrup.
Let them soak for at least 30 minutes so they plump up and soften before serving warm or at room temperature.

title: Gajar Ka Halwa
desc: Grated carrots slow-cooked in milk and ghee until rich and fudgy, finished with nuts and cardamom.
steps: Heat 1 tbsp ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan and sauté the grated carrots for 5-6 minutes until they soften slightly and smell fragrant.
Pour in the milk and bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered on medium-low heat for 35-40 minutes, stirring often, until the milk is almost completely absorbed and the mixture thickens.
Add the sugar and continue cooking for 8-10 minutes — the mixture will loosen as the sugar melts, then thicken again as it cooks off.
Stir in the khoya, if using, and cook for another 5 minutes until fully incorporated.
In a separate small pan, warm the remaining ghee and lightly toast the chopped nuts for 2 minutes, then stir most of them into the halwa, saving a few for garnish.
Sprinkle over the cardamom powder, mix well, and serve warm topped with the reserved nuts.

title: Rice Kheer
desc: Creamy rice pudding simmered slowly in milk with cardamom, saffron, and toasted nuts.
ingredients: 1/4 cup basmati rice, rinsed and soaked 20 minutes
steps: Drain the soaked rice and crush it lightly between your palms — this helps it break down faster and gives the kheer its characteristic creamy texture.
Bring the milk to a boil in a heavy-bottomed pot, then add the crushed rice and reduce the heat to low.
Simmer uncovered for 30-35 minutes, stirring frequently and scraping the sides of the pot, until the rice is completely soft and the milk has thickened and reduced by nearly half.
Stir in the sugar and saffron, and continue simmering for 8-10 minutes until the kheer reaches a thick, pourable consistency — it will thicken further as it cools.
In a small pan, warm the ghee and lightly toast the almonds and pistachios for a minute.
Stir in the cardamom powder and most of the toasted nuts, and serve warm or chilled, garnished with the reserved nuts.

title: Egg Bhurji
desc: Indian-style scrambled eggs cooked with onions, tomatoes, and green chillies — quick, spicy, and filling.
steps: Crack the eggs into a bowl, add a pinch of salt, and whisk lightly just to break the yolks — don't overbeat, a little unevenness gives better texture in the final scramble.
Heat the oil or butter in a pan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and green chillies, and cook for 3-4 minutes until the onion turns soft and lightly golden at the edges.

Add the chopped tomato, turmeric powder, red chilli powder, and salt. Cook for 4-5 minutes, mashing the tomato lightly with your spatula, until it softens into a chunky masala and the oil separates slightly.
Pour the whisked eggs into the pan over the masala. Let them sit undisturbed for 10-15 seconds so the base begins to set.

Using a spatula, gently push and fold the eggs from the edges toward the centre, scrambling them through the masala. Keep the heat on medium-low and stir every few seconds so the eggs cook evenly without browning.
Cook for 2-3 minutes until the eggs are just set but still soft and slightly glossy — they'll continue cooking a little from residual heat once off the stove.
Turn off the heat, scatter over the chopped coriander, and serve hot with buttered toast or paratha.

title: Keema Paratha
desc: Whole wheat flatbread stuffed with spiced minced mutton — a hearty, protein-packed start to the day.
ingredients: 2 cups whole wheat flour, plus extra for dusting
1 tbsp oil, plus extra for cooking the parathas
steps: Knead the whole wheat flour with water, a pinch of salt, and a teaspoon of oil into a smooth, soft dough. Cover it with a damp cloth and let it rest for 20-30 minutes — this relaxes the gluten and makes the parathas easier to roll.
Meanwhile, make the keema filling: heat 1 tbsp oil in a pan over medium heat and add the chopped onion. Cook for 5-6 minutes until golden brown.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add the minced meat, breaking up any lumps with your spatula.

Add the red chilli powder, cumin powder, and salt, and cook uncovered for 12-15 minutes, stirring often, until the meat is fully cooked through and completely dry — any extra moisture will make the paratha soggy and hard to seal, so cook it down well.
Sprinkle in the garam masala and chopped coriander, stir through, and let the filling cool to room temperature before using — warm filling will make the dough tear.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls. Take one ball, dust it in flour, and roll it into a small disc about 4 inches wide. Place 2-3 tablespoons of the cooled keema filling in the centre.
Gather the edges of the disc up and over the filling, pinching them together at the top to seal completely, then gently flatten the stuffed ball with your palm.
Dust the stuffed dough with flour and carefully roll it out into a paratha about 7-8 inches wide, applying even, gentle pressure so the filling doesn't burst through.
Heat a tawa over medium heat. Place the rolled paratha on it and cook for a minute until small bubbles appear on the surface, then flip.

Spread a little ghee on the cooked side, flip again, and spread ghee on the other side too. Press gently with a spatula around the edges and cook, flipping once or twice more, until both sides are golden brown with crisp patches, about 3-4 minutes total.
Repeat with the remaining dough and filling. Serve hot with yogurt or pickle.

title: Home-Style Chicken Curry
desc: Bone-in chicken simmered in a spiced onion-tomato gravy — the everyday curry every Indian household makes differently.
steps: Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the bay leaf, cloves, cardamom, and cinnamon, and fry for 30 seconds until they release their aroma.

Add the sliced onions and cook for 10-12 minutes, stirring frequently, until they turn a deep golden-brown — this slow caramelisation builds the base of the curry, so resist the urge to rush it with high heat.

Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute until the raw smell fades, then add the turmeric, red chilli powder, and coriander powder. Cook the spices for 30-40 seconds, adding a splash of water if they start to catch on the bottom of the pot.
Pour in the pureed tomatoes and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mixture thickens and the oil visibly separates at the edges — this tells you the masala is properly cooked.

Add the chicken pieces and stir well to coat them thoroughly in the masala. Cook on medium-high heat for 5-6 minutes, turning occasionally, until the chicken pieces sear and turn opaque on the outside.

Lower the heat and stir in the whisked yogurt one spoon at a time, mixing continuously so it doesn't split. Add salt, cover, and simmer on low heat for 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is fully cooked and tender and the gravy has thickened around it.
Check the thickest piece of chicken near the bone to confirm it's cooked through — the juices should run clear.
Sprinkle over the garam masala, simmer for another 2 minutes, then garnish with chopped coriander. Serve hot with steamed rice or roti.

title: Bengali Fish Curry (Machher Jhol)
desc: A light, tangy mustard-and-turmeric fish curry, simmered gently so the fish stays whole and tender.
ingredients: 6 pieces rohu or any firm white fish
2 tbsp mustard oil, plus extra for frying
steps: Pat the fish pieces dry and rub them with 1/2 tsp turmeric powder and a little salt. Let them sit for 10 minutes while you prepare the rest.

Heat 3-4 tbsp mustard oil in a kadai over medium-high heat until it just starts to shimmer. Carefully slide in the fish pieces a few at a time and shallow-fry for 2 minutes per side, just until lightly golden — you're not cooking them through yet, only sealing the outside. Remove and set aside on a plate.
In the same oil, add the potato wedges and fry for 4-5 minutes until they pick up a little colour on the edges, then remove and set aside with the fish.
Add a touch more mustard oil to the pan if needed, then add the nigella seeds and green chillies, letting them sizzle for a few seconds.
Add the chopped tomato, remaining turmeric, red chilli powder, and the cumin-coriander powder blend. Cook for 4-5 minutes, mashing the tomato down, until it softens into a loose paste.
Pour in 2 cups of water and bring it to a gentle boil. Add salt to taste, then slide in the fried potato wedges and simmer for 8-10 minutes until the potatoes are nearly tender.

Gently lower the fried fish pieces into the curry, being careful not to break them. Simmer uncovered on low heat for 6-8 minutes, occasionally spooning the curry over the fish rather than stirring, so the pieces stay intact.
Once the fish is cooked through and the curry has thinned to a light, soupy consistency, turn off the heat and let it rest for 5 minutes before serving with steamed rice.

title: Butter Chicken
desc: Tandoor-charred chicken simmered in a rich, buttery tomato-cashew gravy — the restaurant favourite made at home.
ingredients: 600g boneless chicken thighs, cut into chunks
steps: In a bowl, mix the chicken with the yogurt, half the ginger-garlic paste, half the red chilli powder, half the garam masala, and salt. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 1 hour, or ideally overnight, so the meat tenderises and takes on flavour.

Heat a grill pan or regular pan on high heat with a little oil. Sear the marinated chicken pieces in batches for 3-4 minutes per side until charred at the edges and mostly cooked through — this char is what gives butter chicken its distinctive smoky depth. Set the chicken aside.
For the gravy, place the chopped tomatoes, cashews, and onion in a pan with half a cup of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 12-15 minutes until the tomatoes and onion turn completely soft.

Cool slightly, then blend into a very smooth paste. For the silkiest texture, pass it through a fine sieve, pressing with the back of a spoon to extract all the liquid and discard the fibrous solids left behind.
Melt the butter in a pan over medium heat. Add the remaining ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then pour in the strained tomato-cashew gravy carefully as it may splutter.
Add the remaining red chilli powder, salt, and sugar. Simmer the gravy on medium-low heat for 10-12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens and deepens in colour.
Add the seared chicken pieces along with any juices collected on the plate. Simmer for 10-12 minutes until the chicken is fully cooked through and has absorbed the gravy's flavour.
Stir in the crushed kasuri methi and the remaining garam masala, then finish with the fresh cream, swirling it through gently rather than stirring hard.
Simmer for 2 more minutes on low heat, then serve hot with naan or steamed basmati rice.

title: Mutton Rogan Josh
desc: Kashmiri-style mutton slow-cooked in a deep red, yogurt-based gravy fragrant with fennel and whole spices.
ingredients: 2 tbsp Kashmiri red chilli powder (for colour, mild heat)
1 bay leaf, 4 cloves, 4 green cardamom, 1 black cardamom, 1 inch cinnamon
steps: Heat the mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat until lightly smoking, then reduce the heat to medium. Add the bay leaf, cloves, both cardamoms, and cinnamon, frying for 30-40 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced onions and cook for 12-15 minutes, stirring often, until deeply golden brown — Rogan Josh depends on this long, patient browning for its colour and depth.
Add the ginger and garlic pastes and cook for 1-2 minutes until the raw smell disappears completely.
Add the mutton pieces and sear on medium-high heat for 8-10 minutes, turning occasionally, until they're browned on all sides.
Lower the heat and add the Kashmiri red chilli powder, stirring quickly so it toasts without burning — this gives the curry its signature deep red colour without excessive heat.
Reduce the heat further and add the whisked yogurt one spoonful at a time, stirring continuously after each addition to prevent it from curdling. Once fully incorporated, add salt.

Add 1.5 cups of water, cover the pot, and bring to a simmer. Cook on low heat for 45-55 minutes, stirring occasionally and checking the liquid level, until the mutton is completely tender and pulls easily from the bone — mutton needs this long, slow cook to break down properly, so don't rush it with high heat.
Once the meat is tender, stir in the fennel powder, ginger powder, and garam masala. Simmer uncovered for 8-10 minutes to let the gravy thicken to a rich, clinging consistency.
Let the curry rest off the heat for 5-10 minutes before serving — this allows the oil to rise to the top and the flavours to settle. Serve hot with steamed rice or naan.

title: Masala Omelette
desc: A fluffy folded omelette packed with onion, tomato, and green chilli — a quick spiced breakfast staple.
steps: Whisk the eggs in a bowl with the turmeric, salt, and pepper until well combined and slightly frothy.
Stir in the chopped onion, tomato, green chilli, and coriander.
Heat the butter or oil in a small non-stick pan over medium heat until it just begins to foam.
Pour in the egg mixture and let it sit undisturbed for 30-40 seconds until the edges start to set.
Gently lift the edges with a spatula and tilt the pan so any runny egg flows to the sides, cooking for 1-2 more minutes until mostly set.
Fold the omelette in half, cook for another 30 seconds, and serve hot with toast.

title: Chicken Biryani
desc: Layers of fragrant basmati rice and spiced marinated chicken, slow-steamed together until fall-apart tender.
ingredients: 2 onions, thinly sliced and fried crisp
4 tbsp ghee, Whole spices (bay leaf, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves)
steps: Marinate the chicken with yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, biryani masala, half the fried onions, and salt for at least 30 minutes (longer in the fridge is better).
Cook the soaked rice in plenty of salted boiling water with the whole spices until about 70% done, then drain immediately.
Heat 2 tbsp ghee in a heavy pot, add the marinated chicken, and cook uncovered on medium heat for 10-12 minutes until it's about halfway cooked and the marinade has thickened around it.
Layer the parboiled rice evenly over the chicken. Scatter over the remaining fried onions, mint, and coriander, then drizzle the saffron milk and remaining ghee on top.
Cover the pot tightly with a lid, sealing the edge with a strip of dough if needed to trap the steam, and cook on very low heat for 25-30 minutes.
Let the biryani rest off the heat for 10 minutes before opening the lid, then fluff gently from the bottom up so the layers mix, and serve hot with raita.

title: Egg Curry
desc: Hard-boiled eggs simmered in a spiced onion-tomato gravy — a quick, comforting weekday curry.
ingredients: 2 tbsp oil, Chopped coriander to garnish
steps: Make a few shallow slits in the boiled eggs so they soak up the gravy, then lightly pan-fry them in a teaspoon of oil until the surface blisters slightly. Set aside.
Heat the remaining oil in a pan, add the chopped onions, and cook for 8-10 minutes until golden brown.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add the turmeric, red chilli powder, and coriander powder, stirring for 30 seconds.
Pour in the pureed tomatoes and salt, and cook for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the oil separates at the edges.
Add a cup of water to reach your preferred gravy consistency, bring to a simmer, and cook for 8-10 minutes.
Add the fried eggs, sprinkle over the garam masala, and simmer for 3-4 minutes so the eggs absorb the gravy. Garnish with coriander and serve with rice or roti.

title: Kadai Chicken
desc: Chicken tossed with capsicum and onion in a coarsely-ground, freshly roasted spice masala — bold and dry-ish.
ingredients: 2 tbsp coriander seeds, 4 dried red chillies — dry roasted & crushed
Chopped coriander, to garnish, Salt to taste
steps: Dry roast the coriander seeds and dried red chillies in a pan for 2 minutes until fragrant, then cool and crush coarsely in a mortar and pestle — this coarse kadai masala is the dish's signature.
Heat oil in a kadai or wide pan, add the sliced onion, and cook for 6-7 minutes until golden.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add the pureed onion and tomato along with salt. Cook for 10 minutes until the oil separates.
Stir in the crushed kadai masala and cook for 2 minutes to release its aroma.
Add the chicken pieces, coating them well in the masala, and cook covered on medium heat for 15-18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until nearly cooked through.
Add the capsicum chunks and garam masala, and cook uncovered for 5-6 minutes more so the capsicum stays slightly crisp. Garnish with coriander and serve hot with roti.

title: Coconut Prawn Curry
desc: Plump prawns simmered briefly in a coconut milk gravy with curry leaves and tamarind — coastal and quick.
steps: Heat oil in a pan, add the curry leaves, and fry for a few seconds, then add the chopped onion and cook for 6-7 minutes until golden.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and cook for a minute, then add the chopped tomatoes, turmeric, red chilli powder, and coriander powder.
Cook the masala for 8-10 minutes, mashing the tomatoes down, until the oil separates at the edges of the pan.
Stir in the tamarind paste and coconut milk, and bring to a gentle simmer — do not let it boil hard, or the coconut milk may split.
Add the prawns and salt, and cook on medium-low heat for 5-6 minutes only, just until the prawns turn pink and opaque — overcooking will make them rubbery.
Turn off the heat and let the curry rest for a couple of minutes before serving hot with steamed rice.

title: Chicken 65
desc: Deep-fried boneless chicken bites, fiery red and tossed with curry leaves and garlic — a South Indian bar favourite.
ingredients: 1 sprig curry leaves, 4 garlic cloves, chopped
Oil, for deep-frying, Salt to taste
steps: Marinate the chicken with ginger-garlic paste, half the chilli powder, turmeric, salt, and the egg for at least 30 minutes.
Just before frying, mix in the cornflour and rice flour to coat the chicken in a thick, clingy batter.
Heat oil to medium-hot and deep-fry the chicken pieces in batches for 6-7 minutes until golden and cooked through. Drain and set aside.
In a separate pan, heat 1 tbsp oil, add the curry leaves, chopped garlic, and green chillies, and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the remaining chilli powder and toss in the fried chicken, stirring quickly over high heat for 1-2 minutes so every piece is coated in the spiced oil.
Serve immediately while hot and crisp, with lemon wedges on the side.

title: Seekh Kebab
desc: Spiced minced mutton moulded onto skewers and grilled over direct heat until smoky and charred.
ingredients: 1 small onion, finely minced and squeezed dry
1 tbsp oil or melted butter, for basting
steps: Combine the minced mutton with the onion, ginger-garlic paste, green chillies, garam masala, cumin powder, coriander, mint, roasted gram flour, and salt in a bowl.
Knead the mixture with your hands for 4-5 minutes until it becomes sticky and smooth — this binds the kebabs so they don't fall apart on the skewer.
Cover and rest the mixture in the fridge for 20-30 minutes to firm up.
Wet your hands, take a portion of the mixture, and mould it firmly around a flat metal skewer into an elongated sausage shape, pressing out any air pockets.
Grill over hot charcoal or on a stovetop grill pan, turning and basting with oil or butter every couple of minutes, for 10-12 minutes total until evenly charred and cooked through.
Rest for a minute, then slide off the skewers and serve hot with mint chutney and sliced onions.
